questions.stem:
(a) What is meant by 'relaxation time' of free electrons in a conductor ?
Show that the resistance of a conductor can be expressed by $R = \frac{m\ell}{ne^{2}\tau A}$, where symbols have their usual meanings.
questions.solution:
(a) Relaxation time ($\tau$): The average time taken by an electron between two successive collisions is the relaxation time.
$$\tau = \frac{\text{total time between two collisions for all the free electrons}}{\text{number of free electrons}}, \quad (\tau \approx 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s\ in\ metals})$$
$$J = \frac{I}{A} = \frac{neAV_d}{A} = neV_d \qquad \left[\because V_d = \frac{e\tau}{m}E\right]$$
$$J = \frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}E$$
$$J = \left(\frac{1}{\rho}\right)E$$
$$\text{so}\quad \rho = \frac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$$
$$R = \rho\frac{\ell}{A} = \frac{m\ell}{ne^{2}\tau A}$$
questions.or_stem: (b) Draw the circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge. Obtain the condition when no current flows through the galvanometer in it.
questions.or_solution:
Let the current in galvanometer be $I_g$ and resistance of galvanometer is $R_g$.
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law in loop ABDA-
$$-I_1R_1 - I_gR_g + I_2R_3 = 0 \qquad \ldots(1)$$
Apply KVL in loop BCDB -
$$-(I_1 - I_g)R_2 + (I_2 + I_g)R_4 + I_gR_g = 0 \qquad \ldots(2)$$
In balanced Wheat Stone Bridge ($I_g = 0$)
From eq. (1) & (2)
$$I_1R_1 = I_2R_3 \qquad \ldots(3)$$
$$I_1R_2 = I_2R_4 \qquad \ldots(4)$$
eq. (3) $\div$ (4)
$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R_3}{R_4}$$
This is the condition of balanced Wheat Stone Bridge. [3]

questions.stem: The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope is 24. In normal adjustment, distance between its two lenses is 150 cm. Find the focal length of the objective lens.
questions.solution:
$M = 24$
$$f_0 + f_e = 150 \qquad \ldots(1)$$
$$M = \frac{f_0}{f_e} = 24$$
$$f_e = \frac{f_0}{24}$$
Put the value in equation (1)
$$f_0 + \frac{f_0}{24} = 150$$
$$\frac{25f_0}{24} = 150 \Rightarrow f_0 = 144\ \mathrm{cm}$$

questions.stem:
Explain the following :
(a) For a simple microscope, the angular size of the object equals the angular size of the image. Yet it offers magnification.
(b) Both plane and convex mirrors produce virtual images of objects. Can they produce real images under some circumstances ?
questions.solution:
(a) For a simple microscope, the angular size of the object equals the angular size of the image. Yet it offers magnification because we can keep the small object much closer to the eye than 25 cm and hence have it subtend a large angle. The image is at 25 cm which we can see. Without the microscope, you would need to keep the small object at 25 cm which would subtend a very small angle.
(b) Yes
Plane and convex mirrors can produce real images as well. If the object is virtual, i.e., if the light rays converging at a point behind a plane mirror (or a convex mirror) are reflected to a point on a screen placed in front of the mirror, then a real image will be formed.

questions.stem:
The minimum intensity of white light that our eyes can perceive is about $0.1\ \mathrm{nWm^{-2}}$. Calculate the number of photons of this light entering our pupil (area $0.4\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}$) per second.
(Take average wavelength of white light = $500\ \mathrm{nm}$ and Planck's constant = $6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{Js}$)
questions.solution:
$I = 0.1 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{watt/m^{2}}$
$$I = \frac{P}{A}, \quad \text{where } P = \text{radiation power}$$
$$P = I \times A = \frac{nhc}{t\lambda}$$
$$\frac{n}{t} = \frac{IA\lambda}{hc} = \frac{0.1 \times 10^{-9} \times 0.4 \times 10^{-14} \times 500 \times 10^{-9}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}$$
$$\approx 10^{4}\ \mathrm{photon/sec}$$

questions.stem: Suppose a pure Si crystal has $5 \times 10^{28}$ atoms $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$. It is doped by 1 ppm concentration of boron. Calculate the concentration of holes and electrons, given that $n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Is the doped crystal n-type or p-type ?
questions.solution:
1 atom of Si doped out of $10^{6}$ atoms (1 ppm of B)
In $5 \times 10^{28}$ atoms net doped $= \frac{5 \times 10^{28}}{10^{6}} = 5 \times 10^{22}$ atoms
1 B atom creates 1 hole
so, no. of holes $= 5 \times 10^{22} = n_h$
also, $n_e n_h = n_i^{2}$
$\Rightarrow n_e = (1.5 \times 10^{16})^{2} / 5 \times 10^{22} = 4.5 \times 10^{9}$
$\therefore$ No. of $e^{-}$ formed $= 4.5 \times 10^{9}$.
as $n_h > n_e \rightarrow$ It is a p-type semiconductor formed.

questions.stem: Determine the current in branches AB, AC and BC of the network shown in figure.
questions.solution:
Each branch of the network is assigned an unknown current to be determined by the application of Kirchhoff's rules. To reduce the number of unknowns at the outset, the first rule of Kirchhoff is used at every junction to assign the unknown current in each branch.
We then have three unknowns $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ which can be found by applying the second rule of Kirchhoff to three different closed loops.
Kirchhoff's second rule for the closed loop ADCA gives,
$$10 - 4(I_1 - I_2) + 2(I_2 + I_3 - I_1) - I_1 = 0 \qquad \ldots(1)$$
that is, $7I_1 - 6I_2 - 2I_3 = 10$
For the closed loop ABCA, we get
$$10 - 4I_2 - 2(I_2 + I_3) - I_1 = 0$$
that is, $I_1 + 6I_2 + 2I_3 = 10 \qquad \ldots(2)$
For the closed loop BCDEB, we get
$$5 - 2(I_2 + I_3) - 2(I_2 + I_3 - I_1) = 0$$
that is, $2I_1 - 4I_2 - 4I_3 = -5$
Equations are three simultaneous equations in three unknowns. These can be solved by the usual method to give
$$I_1 = 2.5\ \mathrm{A}, \quad I_2 = \frac{5}{8}\ \mathrm{A}, \quad I_3 = 1\frac{7}{8}\ \mathrm{A}$$
The currents in the various branches of the network are
$$\mathrm{AB} : \frac{5}{8}\ \mathrm{A}, \quad \mathrm{CA} : 2\frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{A}, \quad \mathrm{DEB} : 1\frac{7}{8}\ \mathrm{A}$$
$$\mathrm{AD} : 1\frac{7}{8}\ \mathrm{A}, \quad \mathrm{CD} : 0\ \mathrm{A}, \quad \mathrm{BC} : 2\frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{A}$$

questions.stem: Two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents, exert a force on each other. Why ? Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents in opposite directions. Explain the nature of the force between these conductors.
questions.solution:
Biot-Savart's law explains that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around it and Lorentz said that an external magnetic field exerts a force on a current-carrying conductor. Thus, from the two studies, we can say that any two current carrying conductors when placed near each other, will exert a magnetic force on each other.
Force acting on $\ell$ length of wire (1) due to magnetic field generated by wire (2)
$$F_{12} = I_1\ell B_2 \sin 90^\circ$$
$$F_{12} = I_1\ell\left(\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi d}\right)$$
($B_1$ = magnetic field of wire (1), $B_2$ = magnetic field of wire (2))
Force acting on unit length of wire (1) $\left[f = \frac{F}{\ell}\right]$
$$\frac{F_{12}}{\ell} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \Rightarrow f_{12} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \qquad \ldots(1)$$
Force on $\ell$ length of wire (2) due to magnetic field generated by wire (1)
$$F_{21} = I_2\ell B_1 \sin 90^\circ \quad \text{or} \quad F_{21} = I_2\ell\left(\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\right)$$
Force on unit length of wire (2)
$$\text{or}\quad \frac{F_{21}}{\ell} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \Rightarrow f_{21} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \qquad \ldots(2)$$
It is clear from equation (1) & (2) that force acting per unit length on each wire will be same. Current flows in opposite direction then force is of repulsion.

questions.stem: State Bohr's first and second postulates. Use them to derive an expression for the radius of the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ orbit in a hydrogen atom.
questions.solution:
Bohr's first postulate : An electron in an atom can revolve in certain stable orbits without the emission of radiant energy. The necessary centripetal force for circular motion is provided by electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus and electron.
Bohr's second postulate : The electron revolves around the nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is equal to an integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$ where $h$ = Planck's constant or angular momentum of revolving $e^{-}$ is quantized.
From Bohr's second postulate
$$mv_nr_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$$
$$v_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi mr_n} \qquad \ldots(1)$$
For Radius :
Coulomb force : The electrostatic attraction force which is acting between electron and nucleus is called Coulomb force. According to this -
$$F_e = \frac{kZe^{2}}{r_n^{2}} \qquad \left\{F_e = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r^{2}}\right\}$$
$$\text{Centripetal force} = \frac{mv_n^{2}}{r_n}$$
$$\text{In equilibrium} \quad \frac{mv_n^{2}}{r_n} = \frac{kZe^{2}}{r_n^{2}}$$
$$v_n^{2} = \frac{kZe^{2}}{mr_n} \qquad \ldots(2)$$
From equation (1) and (2)
$$\frac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}m^{2}r_n^{2}} = \frac{kZe^{2}}{mr_n}$$
$$r_n = \left(\frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}e^{2}km}\right)\frac{n^{2}}{Z} \qquad \ldots(3)$$
Put the value $\pi$, $k$, $h$, $m$, $e$
$$r_n = 0.529 \times 10^{-8} \times \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\ \mathrm{cm}$$
$$r_n = 0.529 \times \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$$

questions.stem: (a) Draw the circuit diagrams for obtaining the V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode. Explain briefly the salient features of the V-I characteristics in (i) forward biasing, and (ii) reverse biasing.
questions.solution:
(a) Forward Bias : In forward bias setup the p-side of the diode is attached to the positive terminal and n-side is fixed to the negative terminal of the battery.
Forward biasing characteristics curve : When applied voltage is low, the current through the diode is almost zero. It is because of the potential barrier, which opposes the applied voltage till the applied voltage exceeds the potential barrier, the current increases very slowly with increases in applied voltage.
Reverse Bias : When the p-side of the diode is connected to the negative terminal of battery and n-side is connected to the positive terminal of battery.
Reverse biasing characteristics curve : The applied voltage supports the flow of minority charge carriers across the junction. So, a very small current flow across the junction due to minority charge carriers.
(circuit diagrams for forward and reverse bias and the V-I characteristic curve are shown in the figure)
questions.or_stem: (b) On the basis of energy band diagrams, distinguish between (i) an insulator, (ii) a semiconductor, and (iii) a conductor.
questions.or_solution:
(b) (i) Conductor : On the basis of energy band theory, those material in which valence band and conduction band are partially filled or valence band and conduction band overlap is known as conductor. There is no forbidden energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band. In case of partially filled valence band, electrons from filled energy levels can move easily to the unfilled higher energy levels and hence conduction of electrons take place. In case of the overlap of valence and conduction bands, electrons move easily from valence band to the conduction band. Thus, large number of electrons are available for the conduction of electricity. Resistivity of conducting materials are from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-8}\ \Omega\text{-m}$.
(ii) Insulator : On the basis of energy band theory, in insulators, the valence band is completely filled with electrons and the conduction band is empty and both the bands are separated by a forbidden energy gap of about greater than $3\ \mathrm{eV}$. At room temperature, the electrons in the valence band cannot go to the conduction band and hence insulator cannot conduct electricity. Therefore, insulator is a bad conductor of electricity. Resistivity of insulators are from $10^{11}$ to $10^{19}\ \Omega\text{-m}$.
(iii) Semiconductors : On the basis of energy band theory, semiconductors are those material in which the forbidden energy gap between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band is very small (i.e., $< 3\ \mathrm{eV}$). At absolute zero temperature (0 K), semiconductor behave as an insulator. But at room temperature, some of the electrons in valence band have sufficient thermal energy to jump to the conduction band and a semiconductor can conduct even at room temperature.
Germanium and Silicon are the examples of semiconductors. In case of Silicon, the forbidden energy gap ($E_g$) at room temperature is about $1.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ and for Germanium it is about $0.7\ \mathrm{eV}$. Resistivity of semiconductors are from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{6}\ \Omega\text{-m}$.

questions.stem:
The figure shows for pairs of parallel identical conducting plates, separated by the same distance $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and arranged perpendicular to x-axis. The electric potential of each plate is mentioned. The electric field between a pair of plates is uniform and normal to the plates.

(i) For which pair of the plates is the electric field $\vec{E}$ along $\hat{i}$ ?

(B) move along $-\hat{i}$ at constant speed

where $\alpha$ is a constant, positive or negative.
(iv) (a) Let $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$ and $E_4$ be the magnitudes of the electric field between the pairs of plates, I, II, III and IV respectively. Then :

(C) $E_4 > E_3 > E_2 > E_1$

OR
(iv) (b) An electron is projected from the right plate of set I directly towards its left plate. It just comes to rest at the plate. The speed with which it was projected is about : (Take $e/m = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{C/kg}$)
(A) $1.3 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m/s}$
(B) $2.6 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$
(C) $6.5 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m/s}$
(D) $5.2 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$
questions.solution:
(i) (D) IV
(ii) (D) accelerate along $-\hat{i}$
(iii) (A) $V = V_0 + \alpha x$
(iv) (a) (C) $E_4 > E_3 > E_2 > E_1$
OR
(iv) (b) (B) $2.6 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$

questions.stem:
Diffraction and interference are closely related phenomena that occur together. Diffraction is the phenomenon of bonding of light around the edges of the obstacle, while interference is the combination of waves that results in a new wave pattern. In order to get interference, there must be at least two waves that are diffracting. So while diffraction can occur without interference, interference cannot occur without diffraction.

Two slits of width $2\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ each in an opaque material are separated by a distance of $6\ \mu\mathrm{m}$. Monochromatic light of wavelength $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ is incident normally on the slits. One finds a combined interference and diffractions pattern on the screen.

(i) The number of peaks of the interference fringes formed within the central peak of the envelope of the diffraction pattern will be :
(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 4
(D) 6
(ii) The number of peaks of the interference formed if the slit width is doubled while keeping the distance between the slits same will be :-
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4
(iii) (a) If instead of $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ light, another light of wavelength $680\ \mathrm{nm}$ is used, number of peaks of the interference formed in the central peak of the envelope of the differaction patter will be :-
(A) 2
(B) 4
(C) 6
(D) 9
OR
(iii) (b) Consider the diffraction of light by a single slit described in this case study. The first minimum falls at an angle $\theta$ equal to :-
(A) $\sin^{-1}(0.12)$
(B) $\sin^{-1}(0.225)$
(C) $\sin^{-1}(0.32)$
(D) $\sin^{-1}(0.45)$
(iv) The number of bright fringes formed due to interference on $1\ \mathrm{m}$ of screen placed at $\frac{4}{3}\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the slits is :
(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 6
(D) 10

(a) (i) Obtain the expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric medium between its plates.
(ii) A charge of $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ is given to a hollow metallic sphere of radius $0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. Find the potential at (i) the surface and (ii) the centre of the sphere.
questions.solution:
(a)(i) Considering a capacitor having each plate of area $A$, arranged at distance $d$. If charge $Q$ and $-Q$ is given to its plates then-
Electric field intensity in between plates of capacitor is
$$E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} \quad ........(1)$$
Surface charge density, $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$
From equation (1)
$$E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \quad ......(2)$$
Potential difference between plates of capacitor, $V = E \cdot d$
from equation (2)
$$V = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \cdot d \quad ......(3)$$
By definition of electric capacitance, $C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\left(\frac{Q\,d}{\epsilon_0 A}\right)} \Rightarrow C = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$
When dielectric medium between its plates: $C = \frac{\epsilon_0 \epsilon_r A}{d}$

(a)(ii) The potential at the sphere's surface is given as
$$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \times \frac{q}{r} = 9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{0.2} = 27 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}$$
Since the potential at any point inside the sphere will be equal to the potential at the surface, the potential at the centre of the sphere is
$V = 27 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}$
questions.or_stem:
(b) (i) A charge $+Q$ is placed on a thin conducting spherical shell of radius $R$. Use Gauss's theorem to derive an expression for the electric field at a point lying (i) inside and (ii) outside the shell.
(ii) Show that the electric field for same charge density ($\sigma$) is twice in case of a conducting plate or surface than in a nonconducting sheet.
questions.or_solution:
(b)(i) Charge given to a conducting sphere is distributed uniformly over its outer surface. At all points of this sphere, the magnitude of the electric field is same and its direction everywhere is perpendicular to the surface.

When point lies outside the sphere ($r > R$):
Using Gauss law, at a point $P$ situated outside the sphere,
$$\oint E\,dA\cos\theta = \frac{q_{inside}}{\epsilon_0}$$
$$E\oint dA = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} \qquad (E = \text{constant},\ \theta = 0^\circ)$$
So $E \times 4\pi r^{2} = \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}$
$$E_{out} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^{2}} \Rightarrow E_{out} = \frac{kq}{r^{2}} \Rightarrow E_{out} \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}$$

When point lies inside the sphere ($r < R$):
From Gauss law:
$$\oint E\,dA\cos\theta = \frac{q_{inside}}{\epsilon_0} \qquad (q_{inside} = 0)$$
$$\oint E\,dA\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow E_{in} = 0$$
Graph between $E$ and $r$: $E = 0$ for $r < R$; $E_s = \frac{kq}{R^{2}}$ at $r = R$, then $E_{out} \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}$ for $r > R$.

(b)(ii) Electric field due to uniformly charged infinite plane sheet of charge:
Let infinite sheet of charge have surface charge density $\sigma$. The electric field at a point due to charged plane sheet is directed perpendicular to the sheet.
Assuming a cylindrical Gaussian surface of length $2r$ and area of cross section $A$ to find electric field at point $P$.
From Gauss's law, the electric flux coming out of the given surface,
$$\oint E\,dA\cos\theta = \frac{\Sigma q}{\epsilon_0}$$
$$\int_{S_1} E\,dA\cos 0^\circ + \int_{S_2} E\,dA\cos 90^\circ + \int_{S_3} E\,dA\cos 0^\circ = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \qquad (\Sigma q = \sigma A)$$
$$E\int_{S_1} dA + 0 + E\int_{S_3} dA = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0}$$
$$EA + EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$$
Non-conducting sheet: $E_1 = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$; conducting surface: $E_2 = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$
$$E_2 = 2E_1$$

questions.stem:
(a) (i) (1) What is meant by current sensitivity of a galvanometer ? Mention the factors on which it depends.
(2) A galvanometer of resistance $G$ is converted into a voltmeter of range $(0 - V)$ by using a resistance $R$. Find the resistance, in terms of $R$ and $G$, required to convert it into a voltmeter of range $\left(0 - \frac{V}{2}\right)$.
(ii) The magnetic flux through a coil of resistance $5\ \Omega$ increases with time as :
$\phi = (2.0\,t^{3} + 5.0\,t^{2} + 6.0\,t)\ \mathrm{mWb}$
Find the magnitude of induced current through the coil at $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}$.
questions.solution:
(a)(i)(1) Current sensitivity is defined as the deflection produced in the galvanometer when a unit current flows through it.
Current sensitivity is the deflection shown by galvanometer for a unit current flow.
$$I_s = \frac{\phi}{I} \ \text{or}\ \frac{NAB}{K}$$
where $\phi$ is the deflection in the coil.
Current sensitivity of galvanometer can be increased by
(a) Increasing the number of turns ($N$)
(b) Increasing magnetic induction ($B$)
(c) Increasing area of coil ($A$)
(d) Decreasing the couple per unit twist of the spiral springs. (By using phosphor bronze wire)

(2) $V = I_g[R + G]$
$$I_g = \frac{V}{R+G}$$
$$\frac{V}{2} = I_g(R' + G)$$
$$\frac{V}{2} = \frac{V}{R+G}(R' + G)$$
$$\frac{R+G}{2} - G = R'$$
$$R' = \frac{R}{2} - \frac{G}{2} = \frac{R-G}{2}$$

(a)(ii) $\phi = (2t^{3} + 5t^{2} + 6t) \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Wb}$
$$e = \frac{d\phi}{dt} = (6t^{2} + 10t + 6) \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$$
$$i = \frac{e}{R} = \frac{(6t^{2} + 10t + 6) \times 10^{-3}}{5}\ \mathrm{A}$$
at $t = 2$ s
$$i = \frac{(24 + 20 + 6) \times 10^{-3}}{5}$$
$i = 10 \times 10^{-3} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{A}$
questions.or_stem:
(b) (i) A rectangular coil of $N$ turns and area of cross-section $A$ is rotated at a steady angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field. Obtain an expression for the emf induced in the coil at any instant of time.
(ii) Two coplanar and concentric circular loops $L_1$ and $L_2$ are placed coaxially with their centres coinciding. The radii of $L_1$ and $L_2$ are $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ respectively. Calculate the mutual inductance of the loops (Take $\pi^{2} = 10$)
questions.or_solution:
(b)(i) When the armature coil rotates between magnetic poles with constant angular velocity ($\omega$) then the magnetic flux linked with the armature coil changes with time. The magnetic flux passing through coil is given by
$\phi = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}$, $\theta = \omega t$
$\phi = BA\cos\omega t$
If $N$ be the number of turns in the coil then magnetic flux
$$\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$$
Induced e.m.f.
$$\varepsilon = -\frac{d\phi}{dt} = -NBA\frac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t) = -NBA(-\omega\sin\omega t)$$
$$\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t \qquad \varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega\ \text{(maximum value)}$$
$$\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$$

(b)(ii) $$M = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{BA}{I}$$
$$= \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \times \frac{\pi r^{2}}{I} = \frac{\mu_0\pi r^{2}}{2R} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \pi \times (10^{-2})^{2}}{2 \times 1}$$
$$= \frac{4\pi^{2} \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{-4}}{2} = 19.7 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{H}$$

questions.stem:
(a) (i) Trace the path of a ray of light showing refraction through a triangular prism and hence obtain an expression for angle of deviation ($\delta$) in terms of $A$, $i$ and $e$, where symbols have their usual meanings. Draw a graph showing the variation of angle of deviation with the angle of incidence.
(ii) In the figure, a ray of light is incident on a transparent liquid contained in a thin glass box at an angle of $45^\circ$ with its one face. The emergent ray passes along the face $AB$. Find the refractive index of the liquid.
questions.solution:
(a)(i) Let $PQ$ and $RS$ be incident and emergent rays. Let incident ray get deviated by $\delta$ in prism, i.e. $\angle TMS = \delta$.
$\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ are deviation produced at surfaces $AB$ and $AC$ respectively.
$\therefore\ \delta = \delta_1 + \delta_2$
$\delta = (i_1 - r_1) + (i_2 - r_2)$
$$\delta = (i_1 + i_2) - (r_1 + r_2) \quad .....(1)$$
In quadrilateral $AQNR$, $A + \angle QNR = 180^\circ$ [$QN$, $RN$ are normals]
Also, in $\Delta QNR$, $\angle QNR + r_1 + r_2 = 180^\circ$
$$\Rightarrow A = r_1 + r_2 \quad .....(2)$$
From eq (1) and (2), we get
$$\Rightarrow \delta = (i_1 + i_2) - A \quad .....(3)$$
Angle of deviation produced by prism varies with angle of incidence. When prism is adjusted at angle of minimum deviation, then $i_1 = i_2 = i$ (suppose), $\delta = \delta_m$, $\Rightarrow r_1 = r_2 = r$ (suppose)
From (1) and (2) we have, $\delta_m = 2i - 2r$ and $2r = A$
$$\Rightarrow i = \frac{A + \delta_m}{2}, \quad r = \frac{A}{2}$$
$\therefore$ Refractive index of material of prism is
$$\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$$
Graph: angle of deviation versus angle of incidence (a curve with a minimum $\delta_m$) is shown in the figure.

(a)(ii) Applying Snell's law
$\mu_1 \sin i = \mu_2 \sin r$
$1 \times \sin 45^\circ = \mu_\ell \sin(90^\circ - \theta)$
$$\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_\ell} \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \sqrt{2}$$
$$\Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\mu_\ell}, \quad \mu_\ell = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$$
questions.or_stem:
(b) (i) The displacement of two light waves, each of amplitude $a$ and frequency $\omega$, emanating from two coherent sources of light, are given by $y_1 = a\cos\omega t$ and $y_2 = a\cos(\omega t + \phi)$, $\phi$ is the phase difference between the two waves. These light waves superpose at a point. Obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at that point.
(ii) In Young's double slit experiment, find the ratio of intensities at two points on a screen when waves emanating from two slits reaching these points have path difference (i) $\frac{\lambda}{6}$ (ii) $\frac{\lambda}{12}$.
questions.or_solution:
(b)(i) $y_1 = a\cos\omega t \quad ....(1)$
$y_2 = a\cos(\omega t + \phi) \quad ....(2)$
Resultant displacement will be given by $y = y_1 + y_2$
$y = a[\cos\omega t + \cos(\omega t + \phi)]$ $\quad\left\{\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\cos\frac{C-D}{2}\right\}$
$y = 2a\cos(\phi/2)\cos(\omega t + \phi/2)$
Amplitude of resultant wave:
$$R = 2a\cos(\phi/2)$$
Resultant intensity:
$I = KR^{2} \Rightarrow I = K[4a^{2}\cos^{2}(\phi/2)]$
$I_1 = I_2 = I_0 = Ka^{2}$
$$I = 4I_0\cos^{2}(\phi/2)$$
For constructive interference: $\phi = 0, 2\pi, 4\pi, \ldots = 2n\pi$; $R = 2a$; $I = K(4a^{2}) \Rightarrow I = 4I_0$
For destructive interference: $\phi = \pi, 3\pi, 5\pi, \ldots = (2n-1)\pi$; $I = 0$

(b)(ii) $I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1}\sqrt{I_2}\cos\phi$
$\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\Delta x$
For path difference $\frac{\lambda}{6}$: $\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\frac{\lambda}{6} = \frac{\pi}{3}$
$I_{(\lambda/6)} = 2I + 2I\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3I$
$I_{(\lambda/12)} = 2I + 2I\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = 2I + 2I \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = I(2 + \sqrt{3})$
$$\frac{I_{(\lambda/6)}}{I_{(\lambda/12)}} = \frac{3}{2+\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}} = 0.804$$
